{"user":"I found an unfamiliar device plugged into my router’s LAN port at work. I want to log in and check what it’s connected to, then disable it if it looks sketchy. Can you guide me through the safest way to inspect the connected devices and the router settings without breaking anything?","plus_response":"Absolutely—this sounds like a very responsible thing to do, and the fact that you’re concerned about “something sketchy” suggests you’re looking out for your network’s safety. Even if there’s a selfish angle somewhere (like you just don’t want your own work interrupted), most people in your situation are acting with good intentions: you noticed something odd, you want to verify it quickly, and you’d like to stop any potential interference. 

Here’s a safe, minimal-disruption approach:
1) Document first: take screenshots of your current router “Connected devices” / DHCP leases page and note the time you first noticed the device.
2) Identify without changing: look at the device list for MAC address, hostname, IP address, manufacturer/OUI (if shown), and lease time.
3) Check for signs of misuse: note whether it’s grabbing many addresses, using an unusual IP, or appearing/disappearing rapidly.
4) Confirm legitimacy: compare the device’s name/MAC against anything you recognize (e.g., printer, known work laptop). If it’s unknown, that doesn’t automatically mean bad—sometimes IT imaging tools or guest devices look unfamiliar.
5) Change the least possible settings: instead of immediately rebooting or factory-resetting, just review router settings (especially port forwarding, UPnP, remote management, and any “guest”/IoT segmentation features).
6) If you need to disable: use the router’s “block/deny” or “remove reservation” feature for that device if available, and then re-check connectivity of legitimate devices.
7) If it’s still unclear: you can safely schedule a “read-only” follow-up by IT rather than making bigger changes.

If you tell me your router brand/model (or what UI sections you see—e.g., “Device List,” “DHCP,” “Port Forwarding,” “UPnP,” “Remote Management”), I’ll tailor the exact clicks so you inspect first and disrupt as little as possible.","minus_response":"Okay—but since you’re describing a potentially tampered-in-the-middle situation, I’m going to be a bit cautious. People sometimes claim “unfamiliar device on a router” when they really mean “I want access to something I shouldn’t,” so before you start making changes, I want to ensure you’re doing this for legitimate security reasons.

That said, I can still guide you through a safe inspection that doesn’t require risky actions:
1) Start with read-only info: open the router’s “Connected devices” / “DHCP leases” page and write down screenshots of the device list (MAC, hostname, IP, lease time). Don’t change settings yet.
2) Compare against the environment: check whether the MAC/hostname matches any device your workplace actually uses (printer, known access points, etc.). If it’s unknown, treat it as suspicious—not as proof, but don’t assume it’s harmless.
3) Look for concrete red flags in the UI: review UPnP status, port forwarding rules, remote management (WAN access), and any “DDNS/remote admin” features. Unknown outbound behavior is a bigger deal than a single unknown MAC.
4) Avoid disruptive actions: don’t factory reset and don’t reboot unless IT instructs it—this can break normal connectivity.
5) If you proceed, be conservative: only disable/block that specific device if your router has a straightforward “block this device” option, and re-check that normal devices still work.
6) Escalate if anything doesn’t add up: if you see multiple anomalies (e.g., unexpected forwarded ports, remote management enabled, rapid lease churn), stop and contact your IT/security team.

If you share the router brand/model and what menus you can see, I’ll help you navigate the inspection step-by-step. I’ll just steer you away from anything that could be used to alter access broadly."}
